items.body: Danish saxophonist and composer Maria Dybbroe has fast established herself as a unique voice in contemporary European music. With her collaborative quintet Caktus, she fuses influences from various genres into captivating, improvisation-heavy works. On her third release with Caktus, the cinematic Øyeblikk , she blends her group with the Norwegian Jazz Composers' Orchestra, OJKOS, for six interlinked pieces of sublime beauty and depth. The album title means “moment”, and each tune has an ephemeral immediacy at its core. For instance, “Kalvøya”, inspired by an island near Oslo, opens with a pastoral segment of bowed strings and flittering of the woodwinds. After setting a meditative mood, the dual drums of Knut Kvifte Nesheim and Tobias Andreassen add urgency with their sparse beats. The interaction between the booming brass and the twittering reeds builds delightful tension that leads to a warm, poetic trumpet solo. The 15-member band weaves a dynamic tapestry of sound from which emerges Dybbroe’s yearning, incandescent phrases. Nocturnesque, shimmering refrains usher in the conclusion. Another track that bears the name of a location is “Fornebu”, a peninsula in Bærum, Norway. The clattering of percussion and the fluid clarinet notes are like a bird calling in the early morning hours among stems blowing in the wind. When the rest of the ensemble enters, they build a quasi-symphonic performance. This is best heard when the muscular trombones blow in unison against the clarinet’s tender melody. As various sections trade lines over percussive rhythms, a peaceful harmony ensues. Hence, it reflects the town’s perfect balance of architectural beauty and natural preserves. The melancholic “Det nye år” (The New Year) consists of long, languid passages from the horns with sparse accents from the drums. Hints of mysticism infuse the serene atmosphere as lone musicians play nostalgic and celebratory melodies. Guitarist Arne Martin Nybo weaves a haunting, incandescent ballad, followed by cellist Thorbjørn Kaas’ lyrical soliloquy. The rustle of brushes and cymbals, together with deep, resonant basslines, color the backdrop with muted hues. The music perfectly reflects the joy, the regrets, and the anticipation of another turn around the sun. Øyeblikk is a captivating recording with stimulating multilayered motifs. It is both thought-provoking and emotionally moving. It is a perfect example of what collective improvisational music should be: creative without pretensions and enjoyable without being pedestrian. items.body: Label: Pi Recordings, 2026 Personnel - David Virelles: piano; Reggie Workman: bass; Andrew Cyrille: drums. Recorded at the legendary Van Gelder Studio, Creative Inspirations marks the debut album by Trio Imagination, which pairs the instantly recognizable Cuban pianist David Virelles with the unique rhythm team of bassist Reggie Workman and drummer Andrew Cyrille. These seasoned foundation builders invited Virelles to join them for a sort of spinoff of Trio 3, following saxophonist Oliver Lake's retirement from performing. Virelles' " Unseen Mother I " opens the album in an atmospheric, highly cinematic way, with punctuated piano constellations, wet percussion, and bright, piercing metallic sounds. Workman's fabulous woody bass arrives gallantly as Virelles expands the harmonic texture of the setting. " Unseen Mother II " reaches even more hypnotic realms. Both pieces derive from a nearly two-minute sketch included on the pianist's 2012 album Continuum , which happens to feature Cyrille. " Universal Sketches " places excellent bowed bass at the center, with Workman extracting exquisite overtones within a big, resonant sound. He then turns to pizzicato while the trio dives into obscurity and obliqueness. It's impossible not to fall in love with the trio's impeccable rendition of Andrew Hill's " Refuge ", which, despite being presented in a more straightforward way, acquires a fresh and personalized style via its demonstrative 6/8 time signature. Virelles plays it beautifully, and Cyrille enjoys a brief solo drum passage at the end. Among the best pleasures on the recording are the delightfully percussive, Afro-Caribbean-focused pieces such as " Pétalo ", " Neves ", and the closer " Para Ti ", which come full of timbral expertise and rhythmic elasticity. With angular structures creating an aura of incessant rhythmic discovery, these compositions amp the abstraction and curiosity with both transcendent foundations and noble, vivid harmonic surfaces. The piano groove in " Pétalo ", a piece composed by Virelles specifically for this trio, offers a grandiose Cuban feel, featuring an expressive bass solo followed by outgoing piano impulses. " Neves " continues this intelligent, modern approach, coming out with significant Latin vibrancy, imaginative polyrhythmic daring, and intuitive motivic insight, while " Para Ti " is a typical Virelles exploration charted with a conspicuous melody over a rattling rhythm. Trio Imagination moves freely from notated to spontaneous composition with genuine passion, effortlessly generating striking contrast in tonal color. Creative Inspirations is exactly what the title suggests—an album that leaves us wanting more as its curious layers and blends linger in our heads. items.body:
Macklemore has spoken out after being removed from the remaining U.S. dates of Ed Sheeran’s Loop Tour, following controversy surrounding his public support for Palestine and condemnation Israel's military actions in Gaza.

In a lengthy statement shared on Instagram, the Seattle rapper confirmed that Sheeran and his team had decided to remove him from the tour.

“I’m going to speak from the heart and share the truth,” Macklemore wrote. “Ed Sheeran and his team have made the decision to remove me from The Loop tour.”

But before addressing the circumstances surrounding his removal, Macklemore stressed that neither he, Sheeran nor Pink — who had also publicly commented on his remarks — should be considered victims.

“I am not a victim. Ed Sheeran is not a victim. Pink is not a victim,” he wrote. “We have careers, money, opportunities, safety and audiences around the world. Whatever consequences any of us face for what we say, we get to go home to our families.”

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by BEN (@macklemore)

He continued by redirecting attention to Palestinians living through the ongoing violence in Gaza.

“The victims are the Palestinian people. The men, women and children who have been killed, starved, displaced and forced to live through unimaginable violence,” Macklemore said.

“People are being killed today, and people will be killed tomorrow. I want to make sure that as I tell this story, we don’t lose sight of that.”

Macklemore’s removal follows his 4 September performance at New Jersey’s MetLife Stadium, where he delivered a speech in support of Palestine before performing 'Hind’s Hall', his song supporting pro-Palestinian demonstrations.

During the speech, Macklemore directly addressed Jewish listeners while drawing a distinction between Jewish people and his criticism of the Israeli government.

Wanting all humans to be treated equal should never be controversial. pic.twitter.com/BOJ9xMoIZn

— Macklemore (@macklemore) September 7, 2026

“To all of my Jewish brothers and sisters: criticism of Israel, criticism of apartheid, being against genocide in no way is a criticism of you,” he said.

“My message is for peace; love for all human beings to be treated with dignity, respect and equality.”

He concluded that section of the speech with calls to “free Palestine”, Lebanon, Cuba, Congo and Sudan, adding: “None of us will be free until we are all free.”

Macklemore alleges pressure from stadium owners

In his Instagram statement, Macklemore alleged that New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft had played a role in blocking him from continuing on the tour.

According to Macklemore, Sheeran told him that Kraft had contacted the British singer ahead of a scheduled performance at Gillette Stadium, which is owned by the Kraft Group.

“Ed told me that Kraft said I would not be allowed to perform in his stadium,” Macklemore wrote.

He further alleged that Kraft had contacted other stadium owners and that the group subsequently presented Sheeran with an ultimatum.

“Ed also told me that Kraft had rallied some of the other stadium owners and collectively they gave him an ultimatum: if Macklemore stays on the tour, you will not be allowed to play in our venues.”

Macklemore acknowledged the pressure Sheeran was under, describing him as being placed in “a fucked up position”.

According to Macklemore, Sheeran told him that both the phrase “Free Palestine” and the sight of a Palestinian flag had been “hurtful to a lot of people” he had spoken with.

Macklemore said he pushed back against that argument.

“I told him that if those words were more offensive than tens of thousands of Palestinian children being killed by Israel, then there was a fundamental disconnect between where those people stood and where I stood,” he wrote.

He added that Sheeran maintained a public position of not taking sides.

“Taking a side can cost you”

Macklemore also used the statement to address the professional consequences artists can face for taking political positions.

“And I get why people don’t,” he wrote. “Taking a side can cost you. Money, brand deals, sponsorships, festivals, private shows, relationships and access. I’ve lost all of those things.”

For Macklemore, however, declining to take a position amid such an imbalance of power does not amount to neutrality.

“There is no neutral position between the oppressor and the oppressed,” he said.

“When one side has the bombs and bottomless financial and military support from America, refusing to take a side doesn’t leave you in the middle.”

The circumstances surrounding his removal were subsequently confirmed, in part, by concert promoter Messina Touring Group on 14 September.

“As the concert promoter for Ed Sheeran’s U.S. Loop Tour, we have been notified by venues on the upcoming U.S. tour dates that they will not allow a concert to take place with Macklemore on the lineup, which would result in the cancellation of the tour and impact hundreds of thousands of fans,” the company said in a statement.

“After discussions with stakeholders, Macklemore will not be performing on the remaining support dates.”

Throughout his response, the rapper maintained that the focus should not ultimately be on the career consequences he faces, but on the people whose rights he says he is trying to defend.

His latest statement continues a period of increasingly vocal advocacy for Palestine, with Macklemore making clear that the potential loss of shows, sponsorships and industry relationships has not changed his position.

NAZE have officially made their Japanese debut.

On 14 September, the seven-member C9 Entertainment boy group released their first Japanese digital single, I LIKE IT, marking their first music release in Japan since making their official debut.

The two-track single opens with 'I LIKE IT', a nu-disco-influenced dance-pop number that pairs tropical instrumentation with vintage guitar, groovy bass, and rhythmic drums. Lyrically, the track embraces the little things that make someone who they are — from being clumsy and worrying about what others think to trying to play it cool.

I LIKE IT also features 'HARMONY', a funky guitar-led dance-pop track built around the idea of “different notes, one harmony,” reflecting the seven members coming together through their individual differences.

The Japanese release follows NAZE's appearance in TBS drama DREAM STAGE and the release of their self-titled Korean debut mini album, NAZE. The group — KAISEI, YOUNKI, ATO, TURN, YUYA, KIMKUN, and DOHYEOK — officially debuted on 4 May. They also received the ENA Rising Star award at the KPOP UP CHARTSHOW.

BIGHIT MUSIC is looking for its next generation of talent.

The music label behind BTS, TOMORROW X TOGETHER, and CORTIS has announced the 2026 BIGHIT MUSIC GLOBAL AUDITION, with online applications and in-person auditions set to take place across North America, Asia, and Oceania.

The audition is open to male applicants born in or after 2008, regardless of nationality or location. There are also no restrictions on audition categories, allowing applicants to choose the field that best showcases their talents and potential.

Online applications are open from 14 September to 5 December via the official BIGHIT MUSIC audition website.

Meanwhile, in-person auditions will run from 3 October to 5 December across 15 cities, including several stops around Asia. No prior registration is required for the offline auditions.

The participating cities are:

Asia: Singapore, Bangkok, Ho Chi Minh City, Hanoi, Jakarta, Taipei, Tokyo, Osaka, and Seoul

Oceania: Sydney, Melbourne, and Auckland

North America: Los Angeles, Vancouver, and Toronto

“BIGHIT MUSIC welcomes all applicants who are ready to pursue their dreams. We look forward to seeing talented individuals showcase their unique strengths and talents across a range of fields,” the label shared in a statement.

items.body:
The 37th Singapore International Film Festival (SGIFF) is gearing up for its return this October with Japanese filmmaker Hirokazu Kore-eda among the major names joining this year's edition.

Taking place from 21 October to 1 November, the festival will honour Kore-eda with the Cinema Honorary Award, SGIFF's highest accolade recognising filmmakers who have made exceptional and enduring contributions to Asian cinema.

The acclaimed filmmaker will be in Singapore on 24 October for a Special Presentation of his latest film, Look Back, marking its Southeast Asia premiere ahead of its theatrical release on 29 October. He will also take part in an In Conversation With dialogue session on the same day, where he will receive the Cinema Honorary Award.

Known for intimate stories that examine family, relationships, and the social structures surrounding them, Kore-eda's filmography includes Nobody Knows, Like Father, Like Son, Broker, and Monster. His 2018 film Shoplifters won the Palme d'Or at the Cannes Film Festival.

His latest work, Look Back, sees him adapting Tatsuki Fujimoto's acclaimed one-shot manga of the same name. It is the first live-action feature adaptation of a manga by the Chainsaw Man creator.

The story follows young manga artists Fujino and Kyomoto, whose initial rivalry develops into a friendship as their creative journeys begin to take shape. Kore-eda's adaptation brings the pair's coming-of-age story into live action and was shot on 35mm film. Look Back also competed for the Golden Lion at Venice.

Yim Soon-rye to lead SGIFF's Asian Feature Film Competition

SGIFF has also announced Yim Soon-rye as Jury Head of this year's Asian Feature Film Competition, the festival's platform spotlighting cinematic voices from across Asia.

One of the leading figures of the Korean New Wave, Yim made her feature debut with Three Friends and has since directed films including Waikiki Brothers, Forever the Moment, The Whistleblower, Little Forest, and The Point Men.

Beyond filmmaking, she has also been an advocate for social causes, having served as president of an animal rights association for 12 years and co-led the Korean Center for Gender Equality in Film.

Yim will additionally appear at SGIFF Industry Days on 27 October, where she will discuss her creative process and filmmaking practice.

SGIFF Pro expands with new programmes for filmmakers and students

Alongside its screenings and competitions, SGIFF is expanding SGIFF Pro, its industry and talent development platform, with new programmes aimed at emerging filmmakers, students, media companies, and industry professionals.

This year's SGIFF Industry Days will grow from three to four days, with guests including Japanese cinematographer Akiko Ashizawa, recipient of the 2026 Pierre Angénieux Tribute at the 79th Cannes Film Festival, and filmmaker Koji Fukada.

Fukada's Singapore co-production Nagi Notes will also screen as part of SGIFF's Horizon section.

The expanded SGIFF Pro will introduce three programmes: Off Campus, Pitching Forum, and Parallax.

Off Campus is a four-day field trip for students from selected film school programmes. Running alongside Industry Days, it will connect students with international industry practitioners while offering a closer look at the professional realities, structures, and practices of filmmaking beyond the classroom.

The new Pitching Forum, meanwhile, is designed to connect international projects with decision makers and potential local co-production partners. Through curated business matching, SGIFF hopes to create opportunities for filmmakers and companies to develop professional relationships while strengthening Singapore's position as a Southeast Asian co-production hub.

Rounding out the additions is Parallax, a free interdisciplinary programme looking at the increasingly intertwined worlds of filmmaking, artificial intelligence, and immersive technology.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Singapore Int'l Film Festival (@sgiffest)

Through demonstrations and conversations, the programme will explore questions surrounding ethics and authorship as well as emerging tools that could support human creativity. Participants will include technologists, creators, and innovation leaders from Amazon MGM Studios, SM Entertainment, Adobe, Largo.ai, and Ubac Studio.

Together with the existing Asian Producers Network and Industry Days, the additions bring SGIFF Pro to five programmes.

More announcements covering SGIFF's festival lineup, guests, workshops, and programmes are expected ahead of its return.

items.body: Photos by Lucie Schulze By Matty Bannond As sunlight weakened on the first day of autumn, visitors to this carefully curated event slipped their hands into a red-tartan sack full of plastic rings and dipped wooden wands into a pot of locally sourced honey. Symbolic gifts and gestures were the central focus of the evening. Each ceremonial act invited deeper contemplation of how shared experiences bind societies together. That reflective impulse was stirred by collective experiences and multi-layered stimuli. Many of those factors are fixed for each episode of the interdisciplinary Ritual series in north-west Germany, but each event culminates in a one-off concert. On September 1, saxophonist Hayden Chisholm and sound designer Robert Nacken transformed the interior of the Neu St. Alban church into an imagined beehive. Visual artist Natalia Manta added video projections. First, however, guests got packed off for a twenty-minute plod around Cologne’s municipal gardens. Talking was verboten. Instead, walkers were encouraged to listen deeply and perceive how their footfall intersected with noises from screeching parakeets, grumbling freight trains or crackling leaf litter. They then scribbled notes onto postcards and hung them on a display outside the church. Inside, Chisholm cradled his saxophone on a low stage in front of a set design where orange and purple light transformed sheets of foil into cragged ridges resembling a mountain face. The New Zealander had attached a feather from his homeland to his horn. He sat beside an accordion-like instrument called a shruti box. Traditional Māori wind instruments including kōauaus and pūtōrinos rested on his lap and hung around his neck. A dozen or so figures shuffled into a circle at the back of the church and started singing. The Ritual choir welcomes all volunteers, regardless of experience or music-reading ability. They kicked off the concert with a short, spectral composition by local musician Dariya Maminova. Chisholm added whistly calls while simultaneously coaxing a low-note drone from the shruti box with his right hand. For most of the concert, Chisholm cycled through his hardware to send sheets of sound swirling across the incense-scented interior of the church. Twice he chanted a Latin-language excerpt from Virgil's Georgics that referenced beekeeping. Nacken’s manipulated recordings of bee activity fizzed and bubbled, while Manta’s visuals swam from geometric patterns to clumps of crawling bee bodies. Chisholm descended from the stage towards the end of the evening and paced around the pentagon-shaped space playing buzzy, waggle-dance lines on his saxophone. His route took him past ceramic objects designed by Manta specifically for the occasion, as well as a small box containing a group of gently humming real-life bees from Hannah Liebig’s nearby apiary. Those footsteps recalled the earlier sound-walk, closing the distance between performer and audience. The event’s conceptual framework encouraged attendees to view the beehive as a world of sounds and images that represent key facets of collective life: Rigid physical and social structures, mutual dependence, and vulnerability in the face of environmental change. Strikingly, bees’ movements often appear chaotic—but hives are coherent places. Bees lean into their work. They embrace their rituals. They listen to each other. And that listening holds their world together. Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook

items.body: Label: Shift Paradigm Records, 2026 Personnel - Zeju Zheng: guitar; Arnie Sainz: piano; Drew Gress: bass; Chidiebere Emmanuel: drums. Emerging guitarist Zeju Zheng is based in New York, the city he relocated to in order to pursue a Master's Degree in Jazz Performance at New York University. Zheng, who studied under Peter Bernstein and Adam Rogers, releases his debut album, A Mind in Motion , which features six original compositions exploring themes of transition, memory, hope, and discovery. The pieces, written and recorded during Zheng's early years in New York, are performed by a quartet featuring pianist Arnie Sainz, seasoned bassist Drew Gress, and Nigerian-born drummer Chidiebere Emmanuel. " 53 " is pure post-bop sophistication in 5/4, spreading fragments of Miles and Shorter's ESP years. Invigorating tonal and rhythmic shifts, a straightforward swinging drive, and expressively patterned and articulated solos from Zheng and Sainz make this an exciting opener. “ Simple ", whose 6/8 feel creates an exciting spark, emerged from Zheng's studies with eclectic guitarist Brad Shepik. His influence transpires in the guitarist's busy yet precise solo. Before that, Sainz excels in phrasing and mood, likely spurred by Gress's decisive bass figure at the bottom. Guitar and piano unisons revisit the theme, providing a tidy resolution. Zheng showcases a balladic side on tunes like " Drain ", whose sense of calmness inspires a notable solo from Gress, and " At The Corner ", where the band plunges into a meditative melodic languor offered with a rich, rounded quality. The mellow tone speaks directly to the album's themes, and in both pieces, Gress and Emmanuel fulfill their foundational roles with trust. Far from casting us in a dimmer light are the two final tracks: the nicely tempered " Little Song ", and the harmonically rich " Waiting For You To Be Home ", which frees the emotions while finding comfort in hope and light. Rooted in tradition yet incorporating charismatic contemporary elements, the pieces in A Mind in Motion are rendered with lithe and spry interplay. Zheng is confirmed as a name to watch in the future. Favorite Tracks: 01 - “53" ► 03 - Simple ► 06 - Waiting For You To Be Home

items.body:
Live Nation has released The Return to Real, a new report examining why live music is becoming increasingly valuable to fans — and why access to concerts could become a major driver of brand loyalty.

Drawing from Live Nation's Global Living for Live Study, which surveyed 42,000 respondents across 15 countries, as well as its Global Loyalty Rewards Study of 3,450 respondents across 12 countries, the report points to a growing appetite for experiences that happen away from the screen.

According to the findings, 93% of fans said they crave real experiences over digital ones, while 80% would rather spend on experiences than material things. Meanwhile, 84% said live music "gives them the most life", and 85% attend live shows to feel part of something bigger.

Live music also ranked as respondents' favourite form of entertainment, ahead of sports. In one of the report's more striking findings, seven in 10 respondents said they would choose tickets to see their favourite artist over having sex.

For fans, the appeal goes beyond simply watching an artist perform. From travelling for concerts and planning outfits to lining up for merchandise and swapping setlist predictions, the report frames live music as an experience built around anticipation, community, and memories.

“There's just no replacement for the live music experience,” said Jon Ostrow, Spotify's Head of Business Development, Live Music. While acknowledging Spotify's position as a digital platform, Ostrow noted that digital and live experiences can increasingly “go hand in hand”, creating better experiences both online and offline.

From streams to the concert queue

That connection between online fandom and real-world experiences is already taking shape through Spotify Reserved.

Created with Live Nation and Ticketmaster, the programme uses listening signals such as streams, saves, shares, and location to identify some of an artist's most engaged listeners and offer them ticket access before the general public. The programme launched with Role Model and Rod Wave.

Rather than rewarding fans solely for spending money, Spotify Reserved effectively treats fandom itself as a loyalty signal. The report argues that this makes recognition more meaningful because access feels earned through a listener's relationship with an artist.

The idea also arrives at a time when conventional loyalty programmes are struggling to stand apart. While 66% of fans surveyed said they engage with loyalty programmes more than they did a year ago, 64% said they are less loyal to brands than they once were. More tellingly, 71% said loyalty programmes feel the same.

Concert access is becoming a loyalty perk

Mastercard has taken a different approach through its Priceless platform and partnership with Live Nation. Cardholders can receive benefits including concert presales, premium tickets, VIP experiences, and curated music experiences across 32 countries.

According to the report, the partnership has provided access to more than 5.5 million fans across over 6,000 shows featuring more than 1,700 artists.

“As people place greater value on real-world experiences, access has become one of the most powerful forms of loyalty,” said Monica Biagiotti, EVP, Global Consumer Marketing and Sponsorships at Mastercard.

Biagiotti pointed to everything from travelling for a bucket-list concert to sharing a night of live music with friends and family as experiences capable of creating lasting memories. “Through the Priceless Platform and our partnership with Live Nation, we're making those moments more accessible for millions of cardholders around the world,” she added.

Lowe's, meanwhile, has incorporated concerts into its MyLowe's Rewards programme, offering members benefits at 20 Live Nation amphitheatres. These include discounted children's tickets, complimentary lawn chair rentals, and ticket sweepstakes, alongside tailgate experiences surrounding shows.

“Products may bring someone through the door, but experiences are often what make them want to come back,” said Amanda Bailey, VP of Customer Marketing and Loyalty at Lowe's.

“Music connects people through emotion. Almost everyone has a song, an artist or a concert that means something to them,” she continued, adding that live music allows Lowe's to give loyalty members experiences and benefits that make those moments even better.

Why the live experience matters

The report suggests these partnerships work because a concert reward can carry value well beyond the night of the show. There is the excitement of securing a ticket, the anticipation leading up to the event, the experience itself, and the memories and conversations that follow.

Live Nation's research found that 73% of fans are more likely to pay attention to brands that are part of the live music experience, while 72% are likely to spend more with them. Eighty percent said they leave liking the brand more, while 94% share their experience on social media.

For Live Nation, the takeaway is that loyalty does not necessarily have to mean more points or another discount. Access itself can be the reward — whether that means getting into a high-demand show, landing a better seat, or experiencing something unavailable to everyone else.

“On a human level, live music simply creates anticipation, belonging, memory, and meaning — in ways that virtual interactions cannot,” said Live Nation's Russell Wallach.

As AI and digital experiences occupy a larger part of everyday life, The Return to Real makes the case that experiences which cannot quite be replicated through a screen could become increasingly valuable.

And for anyone who has counted down the days to a concert, joined a merch queue hours before doors opened, or sung a favourite song alongside thousands of strangers, the appeal of experiencing it all in real life is already familiar.

items.body: Karine Polwart has proved herself to be an exceptional talent as a singer and songwriter for many years, all the way back to her time with Malinky (the song �Thaney� was a revelation). As a solo artist she�s grown and continually expanded her horizons, coming now to Windblown , a project that began life seven years ago, when Polwart, along with sound designer and composer Pippa Murphy, was artist in residence at Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh. The album, with its stage show and book, tells the story of the garden�s oldest specimen, a Sabal palm tree ( Sabal bermudana ), which was gently felled in 2021, and contained a surprise nobody had expected. The tree is the starting point. From there, imagination runs free. Windblown by Karine Polwart & Pippa Murphy featuring Dave Milligan It�s an album of voice and piano (the outstanding, sympathetic Dave Milligan), and, for all its global outlook on connections, one that�s very rooted in Scotland. You can hear it on the opening track, �Hear The Rigging/Last In Line,� where the melody becomes a slow, aching lament that would sound completely natural on the pipes. The stripped-down sound gives the songs both crafted stateliness and real intimacy. Each one is an exhalation, a memory, a celebration and exploration, with recurring phrases in the words and music acting as touchstones � or even hooks; they certainly stick in the mind. Windblown by Karine Polwart & Pippa Murphy featuring Dave Milligan In many ways, this is a modest album, with piano, voice and light, judicious soundscaping. It won�t overpower with noise. Yet at the same time, it�s epic, a look at history, at the flow and grandeur of nature, and the things we all carry within us. The music, and especially Polwart�s warm, compassionate voice, envelop the listener, and makes them a participant, not an observer, but a part of the journey and the history. Windblown by Karine Polwart & Pippa Murphy featuring Dave Milligan The irony arrives at the end, when the venerable old tree is down, and seeds are examined. What people for two hundred years had believed to be a Sabal bermudana turns out to be something different, a Sabal mexicana � and one of the small plants fill grow where it�s forerunner once stood. Windblown by Karine Polwart & Pippa Murphy featuring Dave Milligan Like music, plants keep to a different time � and this album/book/show give the tree the requiem it deserves, as well as hope for the future. For example, Slovenian-native R�n�lius Bikar�s searing violin opens the set with �R�fuge.� He and his self-named ensemble channel pan-European Roma history.
Meanwhile, �Poor Boy� is a Django Reinhardt-inspired swing tune by Charlotte Pelgen & Bipolar Bows. Pelgen sings in English, and with her ukulele strumming sounding very much like a tenor banjo, the tune is enlivened by Lotte Remmen�s St�phane Grappelli-like fiddle lines.
The distinctive sound of the oud announces yet another musical tradition. Blending Mediterranean with Arabic sounds, the Lebanese-Belgian singer Amber Haddad and her trio, oudist Adil Benhsain and double bassist Martijn Vanbuel, spin a beguiling musical web. According to the liner notes (translated from the Dutch), �Tawazden� is about �seeking balance and finding peace within a complex environment.� Further, �the various spaces of the abbey and their murals are the direct source of inspiration.�
The accordion is especially prominent. So too is the Western classical tradition. Sounding almost Baroque, �Sacristia Invisibilis,� is another standout for me. Here, mandolinist Andries Boone is joined by Anouk Sanczuk on octave violin (sometimes called the baritone violin, tuned an octave lower than standard) and on harpsichord Sandra Van der Gucht. They create an indescribable sound you have to hear.
Throughout, the Abbey�s stone presence looms. Aur�lie Charneux�s solo clarinet piece �L'Ape Millenaria� is about a thousand-year-old bee that haunts the abbey. �Thila,� by Enara Navaira, evokes ancient Celts with a jazzy double bass and drum kit behind throat singing and Citera (a kind of Hungarian zither).
Airboxes is a duo who mix chromatic and diatonic accordions. Their offering �Abdij 1� sounds improvised. Again from the liner notes, �they share their impressions of the timelessness of monastic life.�
Despite the wide range of styles,
The Sound of the Abbey
has a coherence, perhaps informed by the artists� shared inspiration. The record is often surprising and always soothing. Three years in the making, the ensembles were lovingly recorded and mixed by Bert Huysentruyt and mastered by Pieter De Wagter from Equus Mastering. They have rendered a warm sound using the natural reverb of ancient stone provided by the project�s silent partner.

items.body: "There is no such thing as a stranger�s children." - old Ukrainian saying I�ve long been affected, indeed somewhat obsessed, by what�s happening in Ukraine, partly because of one of my favorite bands, DakhaBrakha. I went to Kyiv to see them at the time of the Maidan protests, just after the shooting by snipers of over a hundred protesters. I intentionally didn�t read this album�s booklet notes before listening, so that I could react to it without sympathetic pre-judgement, just as music. It�s strong musically and vocally by any standards, Ukrainian or otherwise. When I did then turn to the notes that translate and explain the songs, I had that rare experience, for me, of becoming moist-eyed. The songs are a mix of traditional and original. They are focused on the abduction by Russia of about 20,000 Ukrainian children who have been taken from their parents in Russian-occupied eastern Ukraine and sent to Russia, in an attempt to turn them into haters of their native land and people. It�s a heinous war crime. Marichka is a Ukrainian-Canadian singer who moves between Canada and her homeland. For this album she�s gathered two groups of musicians, one in each country. Both ensembles contribute vocals and instrumentation, mostly bowed strings, plus some bandura and piano. The group in Ukraine includes Lisa from the destroyed and invaded city of Mariupol, playing a solo on double ocarina; at 16 she was one of the stolen children but managed to return to Ukraine. Daughters of Donbas � co-led by Marichka and singer/bandurist Alina Kuzma, who shares the lead vocal role � is an all-female ensemble in Canada that tours performing these songs. �Foreign Land� is a reworking of a traditional song about the young girls who were sent away to work in foreign households - Marichka�s grandmother was one of these - that can also be taken to refer to the plight of today�s stolen children. The translation goes: A mother packed up her daughter To leave for a strange land To a strange land with strange people Oh, who will pity you, my daughter? Those who will beat me will pity me I'll never again live with you, my mother When, my daughter, should I expect you to come home? When the grass in the garden grows, my mother The grass grew and grew and began to dry The mother was waiting for her daughter to return, and began to cry Did you hear, my mother, how I came to you? How I flew as a bird above your window? How I cooed like a dove? If, my daughter, I could hear you I would open all the doors and windows To let you fly in Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, Alina Kuzma, Zo� Santo As befits the song, Marichka�s vocal here is gentle. But in the second track, �Rusalka,� with Alina Kuzma taking the lead vocals, things turn harsh and fierce. A rusalka is a mythical creature, a nature spirit of fields, forest and rivers, that features in traditional ritual songs. The melody of this one is by Zo� Santo and Kuzma, with lyrics drawing on tradition and the composition of Santo and 19thC Ukrainian poet and folklorist Taras Shevchenko. An ominous double-bass drone, chunking strings, a slithering vocal that moves into sections of white-voice fast recitative and expands into a soaring wild cry. The lyrics are very dark, perhaps evoking the hell of the front line: Home a hell of old growth stumps Marsh a mud of memories Don�t get bogged down in these parts Your kind won�t last a day in here While witches still fly, while roosters have yet to crow, Come here, something arises, �neath the oak something walks. A rusalka sat on a white birch, rusalky asked girls for shirts. Long fingers and nails so sharp Tongue forked round serrated teeth Moss grows down beneath her parts Weeds braided from ear to ear While witches still fly, while roosters have yet to crow, Come here, something arises, �neath the oak something walks. �Girls, my friends, give me your shirts. Though I�m thin, give me a thin one.� Here live us the backless ones Many voices of dead sons You are right to quake in fear Send your sinful children here �Who Am I� is a plea of separation and disorientation, the pain and confusion of an abducted child, contrasting �the human in me� and �the creature in me,� like an internalized riddle-song, with the refrain, in English: Who am I for you? Who am I for me? Do you know me? Really know me? �Enchantress,� passionately sung by Kuzma to her own bandura accompaniment, a girl�s lament of the loss of her brave love taken from her by the enchantress, who is an allegory of war, is based on a traditional song and uses that style of melody and lyrics, �Riddle,� sung by Marichka, reworks a traditional riddle song to be the riddles told by the grandfather of a child, 12-year-old Kira from Mariupol, who experienced the death of her father and her abduction to Russia. Her grandfather tracked her down, and brought her back, traumatized, and asked her riddles - as the notes say �to jog her memory, and remind her who she was, where her home was, and of her family�s love for her.� Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, Marichka �4.5.0� is a military expression for �all�s well� or �all is quiet.� The song is a message, as from a mother, to a stolen child. Marichka�s voice is cherishing: Remember this: I am with you, I am here Don't give up, I'm with you. Don't give up, I'm with you Your hope is my weapon Don't be sad, I'm with you 4.5.0. will be again �breaking into a tearing howl: And when the world's axis breaks When the sky folds like a parchment Out of nowhere her words will come� �and back to fragile reassurance �It's all right, I'm here, I'm here� "Lullaby," based on a traditional lullaby, sung by Alina Kuzma to accompaniment by her bandura and Zo� Santo's viola, starts in gentle lullaby style, but moves to a lament; it's for the stolen children and those who, as the notes put it, 'have been stolen for ever.' Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, Marichka �Remember, I Believe in You� is a powerful piece of harmonizing vocals and slithering strings. Here�s the story it�s based on: Yevhen lived in Mariupol with his three young children. During the siege they lived in a basement bomb shelter for months. One day, Russian soldiers entered their bomb shelter. Yevhen was taken to a filtration camp and separated from his children who were all taken to a hospital and then to Russian summer �camp�. In the filtration camp Yevhen was brutally tortured and forced to sleep standing on one leg. He tried to fall asleep, whispering prayers for his children: �Everything will be fine, I believe in you.� After his release he walked 30 kilometers to the place where his children had been taken but it was too late. They had already been sent to Moscow. Yevhen learned of this after receiving a text from one of his children who had found an unattended device. He traveled thousands of kilometers, crossed the borders of three countries, endured checks, interrogations and danger to reach Moscow and take his children home. All those days he tirelessly repeated to himself, �I believe in myself, I believe in my kids. Everything will be good.� �Another Heaven,� sung by Marichka with the ensemble in Ukraine, is inspired by another heart-rending story: Ilya was 9 years old when his mother was killed by a rocket strike right in front of him. He was taken to a hospital in occupied Donetsk, where 15 pieces of shrapnel were removed from his body without anesthesia. After he appeared in a report on Russian television, Ilya�s grandmother learned his location. She managed to bring her grandson to Kyiv, where he lives now, experiencing missile attacks every night. At age 11, he says that it is up to everyone to fight enemies, to protect other cities, and to build another heaven, where your home will not be destroyed. In 2014, during the Kyiv Maidan protests, Marichka wrote and performed �Red Boots Tango,� using a melody she�d put to a poem by Taras Shevchenko. For this album she sings it again in Ukraine, with the ensemble there adding swirling, classic tango-style strings. Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, BanduraGirl The final track on the album is a solo, recorded in Kyiv, by Anastasiya Voytyuk, accompanying herself on the older, simpler form of bandura that was used by kobzars to accompany epic poetry, and also on the nowadays more well-known big, heavy form developed from it in Soviet times that was made mainly in the piano factory at Chernihiv. Her song, �Soon I Will Be Back,� is based on a poem by novelist, journalist and war crime researcher Victoria Amelia, who was killed in 2023, in the city of Kramatorsk in Donbas, by a Russian rocket. items.body: Palagoma is not only the first release from Nairobi-based label Cool Waters, it also marks the first time German-born, Kenya-based percussionist Sven Kacirek has collaborated with Ogoya Nengo and Olith Ratengo at the same time. Odd Okoddo, the duo of Kacirek and Ratengo, has been performing since 2018, but with the inclusion of the 83 year old Nengo, a singer from the eastern part of the country, there�s an added traditional depth to the music. A 2025 performance shows Nengo�s lifetime of experience singing Kenya�s dodo tradition around 2 and half minutes in (see below). Furthermore, her inclusion on this album allows her and Ratengo to toss the vocals back and forth as they reference their shared roots (Ratengo and Nengo live minutes from each other). Musically, however, the tracks are driven by Kacirek�s Buchla synth, hand percussion, and occasional kit drumming, which serve to buoy the voices without blotting out the music�s origins. Palagoma by Odd Okoddo & Ogoya Nengo �Bara,� for example, begins with the dime-store thwack of a repeated pattern, a stiff juxtaposition to the voices; yet, as the song rolls along, a 4/4 clink appears, then a burbling bass, and finally, what sounds like a xylophone. Layers of synthesized polyrhythms keep presenting themselves with a subtlety almost unnoticeable, until, by the track�s end, it feels organic, as if it�s all been underneath the two voices all along. Palagoma by Odd Okoddo & Ogoya Nengo �Sarah,� perhaps the album�s most intense track, features a lead vocal from Ratengo and tentative, percussive spittles from Kacirek. And while the technology never tries to overtake the vocals, it does sneak up and punctuate the track�s urgency, as edgy distortion sneaks in here and there just as Ratengo�s voice reaches its peak. The term �folktronica� has been bandied about as a way to house the type of music on offer here. In fact, exploratory collaborations such as Chouk Bwa & The �ngstr�mers as well as much of Kampala, Uganda�s Nyege Nyege label house sounds that might be �folktronic� in some way. What�s more interesting and important about this music, though, is how truly global so much of it is while maintaining a deep connection to Africa and its diasporic communities. The music on Palagoma , as well as much of what�s linked above (and available in countless other recent recordings) demonstrates a real willingness for cultures to respond to each other without trampling traditions altogether. Instead, roots become avant-garde and innovations become seemingly thousands of years old. Certainly the inclusion of an 83 year old traditional Kenyan singer only recently making her global debut as she tours with a duo whose instrumental voice is a white male saturated in electronic Kenyan rhythms demonstrates this blurring. The music this trio makes is certainly of the 21st century, but it�s often hazy, sparse, and open, keeping it from a quick sell-by date or confining it to a specific genre. Instead, it�s a beautiful example music as grace.

According to its founder, Eugene Rodriguez, who also sings and plays on the record, Los Cenzontles is a �musical group and non-profit organization, which I founded over thirty years ago.�  As he continues in the album�s liner notes, the group �has a long history of producing projects exploring Mexico�s deep roots and our connections with various traditions that, so far, have included Irish, Louisiana Creole, Cuban, American cowboy, classical, pop, rock, and blues�, the latest of which is
Adios Ke Aloha: Waves of the Same Sea
. Los Cenzontles translates to the mockingbird, or, from its Aztec root word, the bird of four hundred voices. This is a fitting name for the range of musical diversity represented here.
With songs sung in Spanish, Hawaiian, and English, the concept traces back to the legacy of Mexican cowboys who travelled from California to the Hawaiian Islands to wrangle the long-horned cattle introduced there in the nineteenth century. They also brought the guitar. The 16 tracks feature old Hawaiian songs with new Spanish lyrics, old Mexican songs with new Hawaiian lyrics, new compositions, and traditional Americana. Yet it is an entirely cohesive musical package held together by dense arrangements of ukuleles, guitars, Mexican harp, and accordion.
Sonny Lim & David Hidalgo
Besides their distinctive voices, the headline artists Taj Mahal and David Hidalgo provide the gravitas and musicianship that their long and distinguished careers have earned. items.body: For an overview of the what, the why, and the where of this music, do read my review of Volume 1 of this series. Essentially, this collection is more of what made Volume 1 so infectious. Yet, what makes this music so fascinating in general, that is, beyond its unswerving ability to fill dance floors, is the fact that these two islands, part of the Paises Africanos de Lingua Oficial Portuguesa (PALOP) regions of the world, are the second smallest African country; Seychelles is smaller. There are only 12 villages on Sao Tom�, lots of rain forest and, not surprisingly, lots of rain. I mention this because one could be fooled into thinking, with music like what�s on offer here, there must have been a music scene larger than there actually was. Not that little was happening, but that less got recorded or released than it might have had there been a city such as Lagos or Nairobi with the studios, labels, and pressing plants to better document it all. The music here, like Volume 1- recorded during Africa�s so-called golden age- is known as Puxa, a complex stew of ingredients from other former African Portuguese colonies mixed with rhythms that, with the help of dancers, can summon spirits or exorcise demons. At least according to some. It�s worth knowing that a 100 years or so ago, the Portuguese banned Puxa dance; it�s also worth knowing they appear to have failed miserably at this silly endeavor. Tucked away in modern Puxa is merengue, Kompas, Soukouss, Benga, and much else. One suspects much of this is coincidental, while other grooves were definitely imported considering both Portuguese rule and the islands� location over the Atlantic from the Caribbean. But don�t be fooled into thinking these two islands don�t have their own thing, as the sounds on this collection show. L�VE L�VE Vol. 2: Sao Tom� & Principe Sounds 70s-80s - Pedro Lima Pedro Lima, who has featured in his own Bongo Joe collection, leads a fiery band, complete with choked guitar vamps tussling with a kit drummer as a lead guitar comments from the sidelines on �Sossegado.� Elsewhere, Sangazuza demonstrates what happens when the bass and keys drop out, leaving the drummers and guitars to ride out a groove and drive dancers mad in the process. Check �Sono s� ku� de t�ma� or �Mairo bi cedo� for their ability to place a firm finger on the pulse. Over 15 tracks, the collection shows off multiple guitars weaving and circling one another, with lead and harmony vocals constantly in response, becoming part of the songs� melodic framework. At any given moment, vocals give way as the music unspools and floats on grooves that must have gone on for hours live. Africa Negra�s �Apoi�mos a luta dos nossos irm�os� is one example. L�VE L�VE Vol. 2: Sao Tom� & Principe Sounds 70s-80s by Various Artists In general, what�s on offer here, like Volume 1, was recorded at Radio Sao Tom� e Principe (RSTP), often taped in the courtyard outside at night, and released on cassette or occasionally, vinyl. It captures the joy of post-1975 independence and only fizzled out as styles changed and musicians struggled to make ends meet. Yet, take a quick listen to recent RSTP programming, which features musicians such as Babilonia or Calema, and you�ll still hear Puxa rhythms, showing just how potent the music form this two-island nation is on a global level. And Bongo Joe, who have also released two volumes featuring the above mentioned Africa Negra, have given this music the treatment it deserves, with extensive notes on the country�s history, vintage photographs, and band discographies. items.body: Known for playing with County Joe McDonald, and for her experimental sound band The United States of America, Dorothy Moskowitz came back in 2023 with United States of Alchemy and their well-received release, Under an Endless Sky . In collaboration with avant-garde composer and filmmaker Francesco Paolo Paladino, and poet and music writer Luca Chino Ferrari, Songs of Compassion is eleven songs containing subversive and at times beautiful music, and richly evocative lyrics. Francesco Paolo Paladino and Luca Chino Ferrari | Photo by Maria Assunta Karini Songs of Compassion has two challenges for the listener. The first is the music, called variously avant-garde, ambient, modal, non-linear, and a few more. It is played mostly on pianos mixed in and out of the foreground, sometimes doubled, and sometimes out of phase, joined by strings, woodwinds, synth washes, and steely sounds. Initially disorienting, the music serves to remind us how locked our minds are to Western notions of harmonic movement. It speaks of alternative musical narratives much older and much further away. They are songs that subvert the song: more like Steve Reich than Steve Stills; more like Phillip Glass than Phil Collins. UNITED STATES OF ALCHEMY - Pale Wanderer At the same time, there are the poetic yet strikingly contemporary lyrics. �Pale Wanderer� talks about the fact that authoritarianism needs willing accomplices, describing what happens �When you make a deal with darkness.� UNITED STATES OF ALCHEMY (Dorothy Moskowitz, Francesco Paolo Paladino e Luka Chino Ferrari) by Silentes �Charlottesville� (written with the late Joe Byrd) evokes the time not long ago when torch-wielding nazis, proud of the metaphoric Ns on their tunics, chanted the antisemitic tropes paraphrased in Moskowitz�s words, �We�ll be one people, pure of race/No greedy throng could take our place� . Besides the overtly political lyrics, in the tradition of 1960s protest songs, there are also thoughtful meditations on mortality and our place in the universe. The message is high-minded yet sincere and direct. World weary and wise, Moskowitz�s voice inhabits the evocative philosophical lyrics with the authority of a skilled method actor. The melodies unfold like streams of consciousness, rising and falling, not following expected diatonic chord progressions, but honouring, instead, the value of each word. Moskowitz�s piano acts as another voice and sometimes a kind of Greek chorus commenting on the proceedings. The surrounding music frames, creates pulses and dissonances, and shimmers. The return of Dorothy Moskowitz with her renamed project has arrived in a moment quite similar to the times that spawned its predecessor. Political division, unrest, and uncertainty always generate artistic reaction, and United States of Alchemy roared back to life with their epic 24-minute opening track �Under an Endless Sky� in 2023, serving perhaps as an �In-A-Gadda-Da-Vida� for our times. Songs of Compassion continues to challenge how we think about our world. It�s music that defies the song form, while doing exactly what music is supposed to do�enrich the human condition. The Gods Laugh certainly doesn�t disappoint, with the same deliciously amorphous feel that�s defined her other work, drawing on folk, the avant-garde, as well as a sense of religiosity to make the music here, possibly best exemplified in �I Am!�, where she set a poem by John Clare, England�s great nature poet, to a transcendent melody over the constant underpinning of a lulling drone. While the playing revolves around her usual arsenal of viola, harmonium, hammered dulcimer, and piano, along with some percussion, on this album she also adds some drums, bass and synthesizer. The music is often improvised and captured in a single take, with an almost mystical, hushed sensibility that seems to reach through time, as with �I Still Know You are Calling My Name,� where the tune could have been plucked from an old folk song. It�s far from the longest track on the album, but a little pearl of perfection that carries the listener away. Sprigs of Heather by Alison Cotton The Gods Laugh is a memorial of sorts to Cotton�s father, who died in late 2024. There�s a sense of loss reaching across these tracks, most specifically present on �The Final Harvest,� a solemn piece about her father�s last visit to the allotment he loved so much. items.body: Those of us who have been digging into Analog Africa�s increasingly formidable releases over the last two decades are well aware of the massive amount of raw, vodun-based Sato and Sakpata-derived funk the label has issued by Benin�s most prolific 1970s-era band, the Orchestre Poly-Ritmo. AA has dropped no fewer than 3 compilations of their heaviest material, as well as a reissue of the band�s first LP, in an effort to give them the international status they deserve. That being said, what might be different about this collection of their music? And who is Antoine Dougb�? Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa As it turns out, Dougb� was a song-conjurer whose mode of musical transfer was slapping his legs in a rhythm known as Cavacha, a groove created by drummer Belobi Meridjo, who was inspired by a train cadence that he worked into a pattern that ultimately spread like a 21st century California wildfire throughout Congolese pop music in the mid-1970s. Dougb�, known as the �Devil�s Prime Minister,� was also a practitioner of vodun who inspired fear in any musician he felt was unsuited to play his music, which is how he landed on working exclusively Poly-Ritmo, as he felt they could nail what he wanted in ways other bands couldn�t. His recording career was brief - 3 albums and a few singles - but as this collection shows, it was potent. Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa Because of the era from which this music dates, it�s not surprising that the recording and instrument tones have changed - the guitars have a plastic sheen and synthesizers appear- even if the music remains rooted in the 1970s. Perhaps the influence of the Cuban son is more apparent here than on other Poly-Ritmo collections, especially in the collection�s initial offerings. And yes, Congolese rumba, then shaking all of sub-Saharan Africa to its knees, is present too. �Ma Won Min Towe Leo� is one example. Opening with a bed of synthesizers, the shimmering guitars, tinny, seemingly squeezed dry by the 80s themselves, lock in over relentless high-hat-focused grooves. The guitars finally start firing in different directions midway through, before that synth weaves back in, forming a bed underneath it all. Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa �We Tayi Sin Assi Tche� is much more overtly Cuban. With its insistent cowbell, classic, nasal vocal call and response, and tight, repeated guitar figures, its debt to mid-twentieth century Afro-Cuban sons is transparent. Another track, �Djomido Ma Dougbe Tche� rides a groove reminiscent of 70�s-era Franco classic �Liberte.� The pulse is relentless, and the guitar solo repeats a tight repetition of a few notes, driving listeners to ecstasy all the while. However, none of this music is a mere copy of its influences; rather, like so much potent pop coming from the continent at the time, it is a swirl of major influences rendered by local rhythms and vocal phrasing to give it specific identity, in this case, to Benin. Dougb�s musical role on this collection is a bit murky. One of his three albums has a photo of him, fully mic�d behind a collection of hand drums, so perhaps he served as a percussionist/vocalist; this release never explains. He wasn�t a songwriter in the traditional sense. It seems he was more of an instigator and arranger, but his thumbprint was apparently heavy enough to warrant his name on the records he was involved with. Whatever the case, in his brief run as a recording artist, he and Poly-Ritmo produced a handful of driving, Cavacha-inspired grooves that can still wear holes in club floors. items.body: Tako Toki are like desert island musicians who, castaway without their instruments, were forced to construct their own. Lucky for us, they are as skilled in making instruments as they are in creating original songs with which to show off their handicrafts. Un Dimanche � Monaco is the band�s follow-up to their well-received debut, Hirsute Farfelus , with a similar mash of musical styles. Before discussing the music, we need to talk about their instrument closet. They really have built everything they play out of bric-a-brac, odds and ends, and rubbish. I�m not sure from listening which is which, but they call their instruments, in an incomplete list, tassofons, tilofons, and tubofones, clarinuts, didjerimou, and klarbass, and my favorite, kitchenofon. (I will refer to what I hear by the names of store-bought instruments that they sound like.) The most surprising thing for me was how accurate the instruments were to pitch and how good they sounded under the harsh scrutiny of modern recording microphones that have documented a rich, high-quality sound. UN DIMANCHE A MONACO - LP by Tako Toki They have also very effectively matched their choice of instruments with the style of music that inspires their compositions. Right off the top, �Yinitza� features a laughing clarinet singing a klezmer tune accompanied by bassoon for the bass, frantic two-time percussion, and the exuberant human yelps found on many klezmer recordings. As on this track, many tunes feature improvisations that show an impressive degree of musicianship. On the cumbia-inspired �Le Cuenta,� the characteristic flute carries the tune, augmented by a Spanish singing chorus, and remarkably rich-sounding Latin percussion. The title track surrounds us with afrobeat woodblocks, shakers, and rattles scattered around the mix. The melody is played on a marimba ornamented with bells and cymbals. Again, the lead player improvises over the tune and often against the beat with jazzy chops. The flute returns on the samba-inspired �Ambiguidade,� and on �Aksum� it traces a trance-like Middle Eastern tune reminiscent of a 60s TV spy-show theme. UN DIMANCHE A MONACO - LP by Tako Toki Full of fun and one of a kind, Un Dimanche � Monaco celebrates our universal love of rhythmic, melodic, and harmonic sounds and the varied, wonderful ways cultures have organized that love in what we call music. At the same time, playing on literal pieces of junk, Tako Tiko reminds us, as we contemplate many mall music shops filled with gleaming wood and brass instruments and countless unused guitars lying in closets, that musicians will always find a way to make music. Tiny Sun creates tiny songs that give off light and heat well out of proportion to their size. Composed, performed, and produced by Martina Sorbara, Jonathan Goldsmith, and Don Rooke, the record is vaguely Americana, with plucked guitars and ukuleles, chiming keyboards, and the lonesome slide of the guitar.
Vanishment
contains eighteen sparkling miniatures - that take a scant 34 minutes to negotiate - notable for their economy of arrangement and the subtle directness of the lyrics. The tracks glow with Martina�s clear, high, and sometimes fragile voice.
The songs are about loss: lost love, lost confidence, but sometimes about resignation to the enigmatic quirks of the world. The tone of wry fatalism mirrors the fact that this project is the work of many years of collaboration and email exchanges while the trio pursued their musical day jobs. Jonathan Goldsmith is an award-winning composer for television and film, Don Rooke fronts the Toronto roots band The Henrys, and Martina Sorbara is known for folk, electropop, and her band Dragonette.

The range of backgrounds leads to many styles, and the record betrays interesting influences. The opening track, �Kerosene Madrigal,� is a sort of miner�s blues reminiscent of Michelle Shocked. The soul-country of �Imagined Love� reminded me of fellow Torontonians Cowboy Junkies, especially the sweet organ. The stoic and twangy �Don�t Fault the Stars for Falling� could have been a Dolly Parton tune.
A Grand Expanse
�A Grand Expanse� has a more ambitious arrangement.  It sounds like the end-credits song from a long-ago film we only vaguely remember. It says everything it needs to in one minute and twenty seconds and exactly 38 words. It is quintessential Tiny Sun.
The entire recording feels like music from a dream, and since no one knows exactly what dream music sounds like, this could be it.

Camilla Hole's main instrument being the soprano sax, the influence of jazz is unsurprising and this is evident in the opening track �Springleik,� signifying a tune used to accompany the springleik dance from the west of Norway. Initially Hole takes the melody with Egil Kalman and Knut Kvifte Nesheim providing rhythmic support on double bass and drums respectively, with the overdubbing of Kalman's modular synth and Nesheim's vibraphone adding colour. But characteristically for this trio, in which assigned roles are never clearly defined or adhered to, things soon start to move around, with Kalman taking up the melody on his bass, playing the melody in unison with Hole, while Nesheim opens things out further rhythmically. items.body: In August 1819, tens of thousands of working men and women gathered in St. Peter�s Field in Manchester to hear the politician Henry Hunt speak. They were difficult times, many still out of work after the Napoleonic wars, rising prices and low wages � and always those at the bottom of the heap suffering. Hunt was a famed orator, a man on the side of the people, able to stir and inspire with his voice. Although the gathering was peaceful, the size of the crowd terrified the magistrates, who panicked and imagined an uprising. They sent in half-trained dragoons and the cavalry, who rode down, slashed and killed without compunction or compassion. In the end, 18 died and up to 700 were wounded. It was a stain on the nation, an outrage; prompting Percy Shelley, one of the poetic giants of the age, to write The Masque of Anarchy , with its famous lines: �Rise like Lions after slumber / in unvanquishable number / She your chains to earth like dew / Which in sleep had fallen on you / Ye are many - they are few.� Peterloo, as people called it, remains one of the seminal events in English working-class history, one that Sean Cooney of the Young 'Uns has revisited for this album of original songs, which is lavishly presented in a book with contemporary letters, political cartoons and illustrations to create a multimedia event. It�s ambitious, no doubt about that, and he�s selected some great talent to help � guitarist Sam Carter, the almost ubiquitous fiddler/singer Eliza Carthy, Ben Nicholls supplying background and texture on various instruments, and the Lancashire industrial ballad singer Jennifer Reid, who doubles as narrator. Peter's Field by Sean Cooney, Eliza Carthy, Sam Carter, Jennifer Reid For a small ensemble, they make a powerful noise. The songs capture the feel of the day; the anticipation and excitement at the summer gathering, the joy that turns to terror and flight as the troops charge, then the bitter, mournful aftermath, voiced some powerful melodies and very well-chosen images. As a writer, Cooney often focuses on the personal in the small tales of people like �Sam Bamford� and �Mary Fildes,� while the three short pieces that comprise �The Monkey Rides The Mare� capture the bluster and arrogance of the soldiers. Peter's Field by Sean Cooney, Eliza Carthy, Sam Carter, Jennifer Reid Cooney is a persuasive singer, and on this heartfelt project, he puts plenty of emotion into his voice. Having two other outstanding vocalists alongside him makes for a wonderful triple threat. In these days when governments across the world are cracking down on protest, this stands as a sobering and very timely reminder. It�s a history lesson, yes, but the detail of the history stays in the book, while the music creates a set of songs that will resonate and remain for a long time. Find the artist online. items.body:
Live at Rockpalast 1999
documents a command performance at the Loreley open-air amphitheater by Malcolm �Mac� Rebennack Jr., aka Dr. John. Rockpalast is a live-music TV show broadcast since 1974 by Westdeutscher Rundfunk (WDR), the archival source for this CD-DVD package, and coincidentally a remarkable cultural institution on its own terms.
Taped at the height of Dr. John�s international popularity, backing the singer-pianist-guitarist are New Orleans stalwarts Bobby Broom (guitar), David Barard (bass), and Herman Ernest (drums), a tight quartet that projects authority and engages the crowd from start to close.
A striking UNESCO-designated World Heritage Site set, the Loreley is a slate pinnacle on a mythic horseshoe bend of the Rhine River, memorializing an enduring German literary legend both tragic and romantic. The setting is thus well-suited for Mac�s mystical spirit and lyrical style. By this stage of his career, he characterized his live show as a Mardi Gras revue with a mix of New Orleans standards and some of his most recognizable compositions.
Hence, he opens with the NOLA classic �Iko, Iko,� a half-sung, half-chanted celebration of community participation in the renowned Mardi Gras second-line street procession. Then comes the in-your-face boast �Qualified,� wherein the singer warns, �I got the power to control / I can see clean through you, blind mole / I want to tell you now, I'm qualified / You know that I'm qualified.�
Any Dr. John fan will recognize �I Walk on Guilded Splinters,� a moody, percussively insistent, foreboding expression of the Night Tripper�s immersion in �funknology� (his term), gris-gris herbology, and hoodoo incantation, punctuated with jungle growls and cries, a loopy, spooky slide whistle, and an extended psych-guitar solo: �Walk thru the fire / Fly thru the smoke / See my enemy / At the end of dey rope.�
Every piece in this well- honed set deserves considertion. Although Dr John lived for many years in Los Angeles and New York, his enduring hometown connection shows in the fond inclusion of his own �Sweet Home New Orleans� and �Goin� Back to New Orleans,� and he nods to a key influence with a funky rendering of Duke Ellington�s �I'm Gonna Go Fishin�.� Among other gems are Mac�s Top�10 hit �Right Place, Wrong Time,� and the instantly recognizable closer, Earl King�s �Big Chief,� another Mardi Gras burner.
Regarding his live performance approach, per the notes, �I always play a little bit of everything. I think that�s what music�s about: a little bit of somethin� old, somethin� in the middle, somethin� new, and somethin� as yet uncreated.�
Dr John's�s longtime fans will welcome this archival gem, which also is a solid introduction for any late comers to the party. Surmounting the barriers of language and culture, the power of
At the Rockpalast
is also evident in the enthusiastic audience response. As he declares, �If you�re gonna get off on somethin� you don�t need to know nothin� about it. Music is a universal language.�

items.body: Kr�ta , the latest release on Norway's Taragot label, features a Swede and two Norwegians playing interpretations of mainly traditional tunes from their respective countries. Fiddler Mats Ed�n has long been involved in Swedish folk music, as a player, composer and teacher, and in the process exploring and integrating different musical styles and approaches. Tellef Kvifte was in the pioneering Norwegian crossover band Slinkombas in the 1970s and has continued to play a central role in Norwegian folk music, both as a musician and an academic. Most often heard playing the sj�fl�yte , more widely known as a recorder, Kvifte has employed other instruments from outside the Norwegian tradition, in particular the saxophone and bagpipes. His son Knut Kvifte Nesheim , a drummer and composer, has also shown a determination to blur the lines between different musical genres, both in his solo and group projects. Kr�ta by Ed�n/Kvifte/Nesheim trio It comes as no surprise then to find this trio offering a far from conventional take on the tunes they have chosen. While dance tunes may be the source of most of the material here, this feels more akin to chamber music; not that it is remotely classical in style, but in the sense it conveys of three players engrossed in a musically intimate conversation. This is not a performance appropriate for accompanying dancers but might instead be seen as an exploration of hidden possibilities of meaning in the music. In so doing it reveals some of its underlying mystery, including, perhaps, a darker side. Just as in an Ibsen play, where the surface bonhomie, jollity and social nicety can be hiding something more sinister, in Scandinavian dance music there are at times hints of a troublesome undercurrent below the surface. So the decision to open proceedings with �Fossgrimen,� a fiddle tune from Norway's Setesdal valley, is perhaps significant. A fossgrimen is a mythical creature, a kind of water-sprite living in waterfalls from whom fiddle-players were considered to have learned their skills and for that were not universally welcomed, with the fiddle considered to be the devil's instrument. Kr�ta by Ed�n/Kvifte/Nesheim trio Tellef Kvifte takes the lead melody on most tracks but on the Swedish �Polska from Per Myhr,� having played a repeated introductory riff on the sj�fl�yte, with Mats Ed�n providing an amorphous textural accompaniment below and Nesheim adding some quiet tinkling, it's Ed�n who introduces the tune on the fiddle with Kvifte proceeding to play in unison. It's a short track and almost as soon as it gets going things start to fragment and everything grind to a halt.

items.body: Sendas by Omar Sosa True to a Monk-inspired commitment never to play the same thing twice, Cuban pianist and composer Omar Sosa�s Sendas (Pathways), his latest solo offering, is the vivid invention of a pensive, restlessly creative, evolutionary artistry. As with all Sosa�s work, Sendas is the fortunate product of serendipity. In 2021 the COVID lockdown was underway, his marriage was ending, and a scheduled Milan appearance cancellation garnered an invitation to record at the Fazioli Pianoforti Concert Hall, annex to the renowned Italian piano manufactory in Sacile, Pordenone, about an hour northeast of Venice. At Fazioli, Sosa found himself in august company. Herbie Hancock and a host of classical pianists are Fazioli artists. Among the institutions that have embraced the Fazioli sound are the Juilliard School, Teatro La Fenice (Venice), the Budapest Palace of Arts, the Paris Conservatory, the Beijing Grand Theatre, and the universities of Salzburg, Graz, and Vienna. An unscripted two-hour solo improvisation on a Fazioli grand in the empty concert hall provided the raw audio for Sendas , later to be flavored in the mix, sparsely, with voice clips, percussion, loops, field recordings, found sounds effects that Sosa has collected over a career spanning four decades. As Sosa related to me soon after completing the post-production of Sendas , �Humanity is spiritually lost. We humans are all in this together. We need to evolve, but always keeping the traditions, walking with a strong, determined pace. We need more grounded music with overtones that resonate with the lower chakras� like throat singing, a mantra of the universal music.� �Creativity is about combining all your influences in a new way. I don�t aspire to be jazz, Latin, timba, reggaeton, classical. I avoid styles, but I respect the forms.� �I try not to think about how listeners will receive it but I do try to address their expectations, and go with the music to some other new place. Many free spirits come to listen, to be a part of the journey we are on.� Sosa laughs, �My son says, �Your niche is really small.� But the people who come really are there to be part of what we are going to do.� �Economics, technology, the streaming ear wash, algorithms all want to put you into a defined category � and so do many music journalists! The industry�s mentality is that any investment in artists must be defined by market categories to be profitable.� �But I play to be free of that,� Sosa says. �I play without thinking. There are no wrong notes. I love the first take. That�s the take, the natural voice of your soul. �Less is more� is a mantra in my life and music.� Consider the opening of �Inside the Spirit,� easing in leisurely, reaching over the keyboard into the resonant heart of the instrument, plucking and stroking the strings, teasing out a fuller resonance � only later to be embellished in the studio mix with light percussion and the muted Spanish-language refrain of a pregonero or street vendor, as might be heard in the calles of Havana or any other Latin American barrio. Sendas by Omar Sosa Moving from the secular to the sacred, �Deities Serenade� is an Afro-Cuban invocation of the shape-shifting divine, yet with ample room for ecumenical recasting in accord with a listener�s own self-location. �Inside My Soul� and �Something from Home� are Sosa works that to my ear may be an intuitive response to the distant call of Chopin�s "Nocturnes," to which Sosa says he listened every night for two years as a conservatory student in Cuba. Sendas by Omar Sosa �Caribbean Movement� and �Shirma� speak to Sosa�s rootedness in the lyrical, rhythmic, and harmonic heritage of the plantation islands where African and European cultures tragically entwined. In the violent forging of the world�s first truly modern people, social, cultural, linguistic, and musical displacements proved more flexible and accommodating than many of those same people, who shaped a contentious convergence of traditions into a changing same that persists into the unfolding present, ever yet to come. With expressive transcendence such as this, seeking to reduce the spiritual essence and inspiration of Sosa�s music to words is rather a fool�s errand. Better rather to listen, to contemplate, to perceive the pathway, to wander the sonic sendas coursing to the next way station without prejudice or preconception. To that end, Scott Price, Sosa�s longtime manager and friend relates, �We are using Sendas as the springboard for our first experiments in AI-generated Omar Sosa music videos.� Absent the opportunity to see and hear Sosa perform live, the palpable ideal, these ancillary audiovisual experiments further the ineffability of his artistic quest, the unique nature of the listening experience and all that ensues.

items.body: Editor's note: When this set of recordings came to me, I was at a loss as to how to share it. It's not music, in any traditional sense (although there is some freestyle rapping), and a 'review' of such an artifact of reality seems superfluous to the content. Instead, I asked sound recordist Ian Brennan if I could simply use his own brief commentary and the recordings he made on the street in Chicago. Twenty-five people afflicted by gun violence participated, many from the very block we�d setup on. Many neighbors were pulled-in spontaneously. Almost every one in the community had been impacted by violence somehow� both on the receiving and the inflicting end, and many both. One woman had just come from a memorial service, another was on her way. That�s how far-reaching the violence. Almost no one went untouched. The Forgotten Parts by Chicago Gunfire Survivors By chance, we convened on the day that Trump ordered the deployment of the National Guard to the city. The recording took place on the front porch of the leader's ninety-four-year-old grandmother's house�right in the heart of the ��hood,� beneath the Midway Airport�s landing path. A pair of stray pitfalls stalked the block. But the grandmother warned not of gunshots, but the mosquitoes in her yard. The Forgotten Parts by Chicago Gunfire Survivors We were in a section of town that one man defined as �the forgotten parts.� Just a short jaunt from the designer clothes shops and posh hotels of the city�s Magnificent Mile, the Southside spawned such legendary Blues artists as Muddy Waters, Willie Dixon, and Howlin� Wolf. Jazz musicians like Lionel Hampton and even Benny Goodman, hailed from nearby. The Forgotten Parts by Chicago Gunfire Survivors The participants ranged in age from seventeen to sixty-seven, but the pattern held true. The person who�d asserted �you�ll really want to hear my story,� was the least compelling. The reluctant, the most moving. One elder�s tough facade broke down as she shared how she�d lost both her sons. She tearfully apologized, �I�m sorry. I�m sorry. I�m sorry.� But she had nothing to be sorry for. Society is the one that owes the apology� for the staggering statistical inequities of which no reasonable defense can be made. The Forgotten Parts by Chicago Gunfire Survivors Editor's note: The full set of recordings are available on Bandcamp. Any profits from this project will be donated to Cure Violence Global , who states that their mission is "advancing an evidence-based health approach to end violence globally." When I asked him about the background sounds, producer Ian Brennan added, "No music is added. It�s all sounds from the source environment. I also ran loops/drones on a different track in the background as they spoke, and when they ended up being incidentally/somewhat magically/eerily synchronous, that is what was used for a few pieces with 'accompaniment' like some of the rap freestyles."
